title: Trains to Swansea
from: the main stations in Wales and England
lead: These are the trains I would look at for the Wales Airshow. Swansea station is right in the city centre, about a 20 to 25 minute walk from the seafront. GWR runs a direct train from London Paddington most hours, through Reading, Swindon, Bristol Parkway, Newport and Cardiff, and Transport for Wales brings you in from West Wales, the Marches line and Manchester. I’ve added the connections that work well from Bristol and Birmingham too. Pick your station, a day and a time below and the map shows every station on the way.
facts: Both show days, Saturday and Sunday
Most hours from London, more from Cardiff
ysIntro: This is the station I would get off at for the Wales Airshow. The details below follow the train you pick further down the page.
walkLine: From the station it’s about 20 to 25 minutes on foot. Head down through the city centre to Oystermouth Road and the promenade by the Civic Centre. Oystermouth Road and Mumbles Road are closed on show days, so it’s an easy walk once you’re through town, and you can just follow the crowd.
walkBack: Allow about 25 minutes to walk back up to the station from the seafront, and a fair bit longer when everyone leaves at once.
tip: Trains back to London, Cardiff and Bristol get very busy straight after the flying. I would either leave a little early, or stay in town for something to eat and catch a later train.
If you’re staying for Afterburn on the Saturday evening, look at the last train home before it starts. From the further away stations the last good connection can leave Swansea before the fireworks.
There were engineering works on the airshow weekend in 2026, with fewer GWR trains from London. The summer 2027 times come out nearer the show, so please check before you travel.
tipBtn: Back to getting to the Wales Airshow
alt: When I last checked, an anytime day return from Cardiff was £15.30 and from Llanelli £7.60, so the local trains are cheap.

From London, Reading or Bristol I would book an advance ticket early, as it can save a lot. If you’re going as a family, a Family and Friends Railcard takes a third off adult fares and 60% off children’s fares, so it may well pay for itself on this one trip.
note: Times are from the National Rail timetable for Saturday 7 and Sunday 8 November 2026, checked on 30 October 2026, so they are a guide to how weekend trains run rather than the show weekend times. Some Sunday trains from London were changed by engineering works that weekend. Times for summer 2027 usually come out in the spring, so please check before you travel. The line is drawn along the railway, so treat it as a guide. Map data © OpenStreetMap contributors.
gaOnly: Transport for Wales and GWR, plus the connections that work well. Most trains into Swansea are run by these two, with CrossCountry helping out from Birmingham. I’ve only included the big stations where the whole trip works on a weekend. If you’re coming from somewhere else, I would plan your trip to one of these stations first and pick it up from there.

about.London Paddington|Reading: Out of Paddington along Brunel’s Great Western, through the west London suburbs and past Slough.
about.Reading|Swindon: Through Didcot, past the cooling towers site, and along the Vale of the White Horse.
about.Swindon|Bristol Parkway: Across the Wiltshire and Gloucestershire countryside, through the Chipping Sodbury tunnel.
about.London Paddington|Swindon: Out along Brunel’s Great Western through Reading and Didcot.
about.Bristol Parkway|Newport: Under the River Severn through the Severn Tunnel, over four miles long, then across the border into Wales.
about.Bristol Parkway|Cardiff Central: Under the River Severn through the Severn Tunnel, then into Wales through Newport.
about.Bristol Temple Meads|Newport: Out through Filton, past the old Concorde site at Filton, then under the River Severn into Wales.
about.Bristol Temple Meads|Bristol Parkway: Through Bristol’s northern suburbs, past Filton, home of the Aerospace Bristol museum and Concorde.
about.Newport|Cardiff Central: A short run along the Gwent Levels into Cardiff, with the Principality Stadium beside the station.
about.Cardiff Central|Bridgend: West through the Vale of Glamorgan countryside, past Pontyclun and Pencoed.
about.Bridgend|Neath: Along the coast past Port Talbot and its steelworks, with Swansea Bay opening up on your left.
about.Bridgend|Swansea: Along the coast past Port Talbot, then round through Neath and into Swansea. Look out over the bay on your left.
about.Neath|Swansea: The last few minutes in, through Skewen and Llansamlet. Swansea is the end of the line, so trains heading west reverse out the way they came.
about.Cardiff Central|Swansea: West through Bridgend and along the coast past Port Talbot, with Swansea Bay on your left.
about.Llanelli|Swansea: Along the Loughor estuary and through Gowerton, with views across to the Gower.
about.Carmarthen|Llanelli: Along the coast past Kidwelly and Ferryside, with the Towy estuary and Carmarthen Bay beside you.
about.Shrewsbury|Hereford: Down the Welsh Marches line through Church Stretton and Ludlow, past the Long Mynd hills.
about.Hereford|Newport: Through Abergavenny, with the Black Mountains to the west.
about.Crewe|Shrewsbury: Through the Cheshire and Shropshire countryside, past Nantwich, Whitchurch and Wem.
about.Manchester Piccadilly|Crewe: South through Stockport and Wilmslow, across the Cheshire plain.
about.Birmingham New Street|Cheltenham Spa: Down the Lickey Incline, the steepest main line in Britain, and past Worcestershire Parkway.
about.Cheltenham Spa|Gloucester: A short hop, with the Cotswolds off to the east.
about.Gloucester|Newport: Along the Severn estuary through Lydney and Chepstow, crossing the River Wye into Wales.
